definition: The Fireworks Algorithm (FWA) is a swarm intelligence algorithm that explores a very large solution space by choosing a set of random points confined by some distance metric in the hopes that one or more of them will yield promising results, allowing for a more concentrated search nearby..
details: The Fireworks Algorithm (FWA) is a swarm intelligence algorithm that explores a very large solution space by choosing a set of random points confined by some distance metric in the hopes that one or more of them will yield promising results, allowing for a more concentrated search nearby.

explainer.lead: The Fireworks Algorithm is a search method for problems with far too many possible answers to check one by one. It scatters random test points across the solution space, then searches more closely around points that look promising.

tiers.eli5: Like setting off a firework, seeing where the bright sparks land, then launching smaller fireworks around the brightest spot.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply it to large search spaces, generating random points and then concentrating the search around the best results. The pitfall is the balance of random spread against local intensification: too little spread misses good regions, too much wastes evaluations.
tiers.paperLevel: The algorithm explores a very large solution space by choosing a set of random points confined by some distance metric, then concentrates the search nearby where results are promising. No convergence guarantee is specified.

explainer.example: Suppose the goal is to minimize f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2. Three random candidates give f(4,3) = 25, f(1,2) = 5, and f(-2,1) = 5, so the latter two are more promising; the next search can sample points close to them rather than spreading every new point across the whole space.
explainer.goal: Find promising solutions in a very large search space without examining every possibility.
inputs: A way to judge promising points
outputs: A set of evaluated candidate points
steps: Define the solution space and distance limits.
Choose a set of random points within those limits.
Evaluate the points to identify promising results.
Search more densely near the promising points.
tradeoffs: Random points provide broad initial coverage.
Concentrated sampling reuses information from good candidates.
Random placement may miss important regions.
Early promising points can draw search away from better areas.

nodes.label: Nearby search
nodes.note: More concentrated sampling around those seeds

diagram.caption: FWA moves from scattered candidate points to concentrated search around promising results.
